w:r.w:t: The Step Noise Detection application is a Python desktop tool for analyzing baseline data from TDD files produced by Nabsys HD-Mapping instruments. It reads interleaved multi-channel voltage data (typically 256 channels at 100 Hz), detects step noise using four complementary methods, and provides interactive visualization for inspecting results.

Step noise is a characteristic interference pattern where the signal abruptly rises by some amplitude, holds at an elevated level for a period, then falls back. It can be periodic or intermittent, varies in amplitude and duration, and may appear on one channel or propagate as crosstalk to physically adjacent channels.

The Envelope tab implements the “hug” detector ported from the MATLAB StepNoiseCalculator.m script. It provides a complementary view of step noise by analyzing how closely the signal hugs its upper and lower envelopes versus its overall mean.
When the Envelope tab is active and a channel is selected, the application computes upper and lower signal envelopes and calculates per-sample distances. The plot displays:
shown as dashed lines tracing the signal’s peaks and troughs.

The plot title reports the key metric: the hug/mid ratio. A ratio less than 1.0 indicates step noise (the data clusters near the envelopes rather than the center). The closer the ratio is to zero, the stronger the bimodal step-noise pattern.

The peak separation parameter (default 50 samples) controls the smoothness of the envelopes. Higher values produce smoother envelopes; lower values track rapid fluctuations more closely. The analysis automatically re-runs when the active channel changes.
Displays the power spectral density of the selected channel, computed in time chunks.
The plot shows frequency (Hz) on the x-axis and power (dB) on the y-axis. Periodic step noise appears as distinct peaks at the fundamental frequency and its harmonics.
Automatically identify time regions with elevated noise levels without requiring manual threshold tuning for the absolute signal level.

Compute a sliding-window Root Mean Square (RMS) of the channel signal. The window size is configurable (default 1 second). For each sample position, the RMS is the square root of the mean of the squared signal values within the window centered on that position.
Estimate the baseline noise level as the 25th percentile of all RMS values. This represents the typical quiet-state noise floor, assuming that most of the recording is noise-free.
Set a detection threshold at baseline × threshold_multiplier (default 3.0×).
Flag all contiguous regions where the sliding RMS exceeds the threshold as noise segments.
Report the baseline RMS, threshold, list of noisy segments (start time, end time, mean RMS), and the overall noise fraction (percentage of total recording time that was flagged).

Controls the time resolution of the RMS envelope. A 1-second window smooths out individual sample noise and responds to sustained changes. Shorter windows are more sensitive to brief events; longer windows average them out.

How many times the baseline a segment’s RMS must exceed. A value of 3.0 means the noise must be 3× louder than normal to be flagged. Lower values catch more subtle noise but may produce false positives.
As a first-pass scan to identify which time regions contain anomalous signal levels. Works well for noise that is significantly louder than the baseline, regardless of its waveform shape.
Detect step noise specifically — abrupt signal jumps (rising edge) followed by a return to baseline (falling edge), with a measurable plateau between them.

Apply Savitzky-Golay smoothing (polynomial order 2) to the raw signal to stabilize the numerical derivative while preserving step edges. The smoothing window length scales with sample rate (approximately 50 ms, capped at 101 samples).
Compute the first derivative (sample-to-sample difference) of the smoothed signal.

Scan the derivative for positive excursions exceeding half the amplitude threshold. When found, track the rising edge from start to end and compute the step amplitude (signal level after rise minus signal level before rise).

If the rising step amplitude meets the full amplitude threshold, search forward within the maximum width window for a corresponding falling edge — a negative excursion in the derivative whose amplitude is at least 40% of the rising step.
If a matching falling edge is found and the plateau width (time between end of rise and start of fall) falls within [min width, max width], record the event.
Each event records: start sample, end sample, amplitude in microvolts, and plateau width in samples.
Minimum step height. Only steps taller than this value are detected. Default: 50.0 µV.
Minimum time the signal must remain elevated before falling back. Filters out brief transients. Default: 0.05 s.
Maximum time between rise and fall. Events longer than this are not considered step noise. Default: 60.0 s.

When you suspect step noise (rectangular pulse-like interference). This method is shape-specific — it looks for the rise-plateau-fall pattern rather than just elevated amplitude. It provides precise timing, amplitude, and duration for each event.
Reveal periodic components in the signal that may indicate repetitive step noise. If step noise occurs at a regular interval, it produces characteristic peaks in the frequency domain.
Divide the channel signal into consecutive time chunks (default 5 minutes each).
For each chunk, apply a spectral window function (default: Hann window) to reduce spectral leakage at the chunk boundaries.
Compute the real-valued FFT of the windowed chunk.
Calculate the power spectral density as |FFT|² normalized by the window energy, converted to decibels (dB).
Display frequency on the x-axis and power in dB on the y-axis.
Length of each time segment. Longer chunks give better frequency resolution but worse time resolution. Default: 5 minutes.
The spectral window applied before FFT. See window comparison table below.
Upper frequency limit for the display. Set to 0 to show full range up to Nyquist.
Similar to Hann, different sidelobe behavior
Very low sidelobes, wider main lobe
Detecting weak peaks near strong ones

A clean signal shows a relatively flat noise floor. Periodic step noise produces a sharp peak at its repetition frequency plus harmonics (peaks at 2×, 3×, etc.). Compare chunks to see if the noise is constant or intermittent.

The envelope/hug detector is ported from the MATLAB StepNoiseCalculator.m script. It provides a statistical measure of whether the signal exhibits bimodal (step-like) behavior by comparing how closely data points cluster near the signal’s envelopes versus its overall mean.

Find local peaks (for the upper envelope) and local troughs (for the lower envelope) using scipy.signal.find_peaks with a minimum peak separation parameter (default 50 samples). Interpolate between these peak/trough positions to produce smooth, full-length envelope curves.
For each sample, compute the absolute distance to both the upper and lower envelopes, then take the minimum. This “hug” value measures how close each data point is to its nearest envelope.
For each sample, compute the absolute distance to the overall signal mean.
ratio = mean(hug) / mean(mid). This single scalar summarizes the result.
— The signal clusters near its envelopes (bimodal distribution). This indicates step noise, where the signal spends most of its time near the “high” or “low” level rather than near the center.
— The signal is roughly uniformly distributed between the envelopes and the mean. No strong step noise pattern.
— The signal clusters near the mean (Gaussian-like noise). This is the expected behavior for a clean baseline.

The envelope method is particularly useful for detecting step noise that the edge detector might miss — for example, when step transitions are gradual or when the signal has many small, closely spaced steps that don’t individually exceed the edge amplitude threshold but collectively produce a bimodal distribution.
TDD files store channel data in a hardware-specific scrambled order. The application descrambles channels and presents them sorted numerically (Ch 1, Ch 2, … Ch 256) in all dropdown selectors.
The physical channel layout on the detector follows a serpentine pattern:
This means physically adjacent channels have IDs that differ by 2 (odd channels ascending, then even channels descending). The application handles this mapping internally.
